cards.front: How are the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile related when air resistance is ignored?
cards.back: They are **independent**. Gravity acts only downwards, so it changes the vertical velocity and leaves the horizontal velocity constant.
cards.hint: Think about which directions the forces act in.

cards.front: Why is the time of flight found from the vertical motion rather than the horizontal motion?
cards.back: Vertical motion has the acceleration, so it gives the **time of flight**. Both motions last the same time, so this time is then used in $s_x=u_xt$.
cards.hint: Which motion has an acceleration in it?

cards.front: What are the steps to find the range of a projectile launched at an angle from level ground?
cards.back: 1) Resolve: $u_x=u\cos\theta$ and $u_y=u\sin\theta$. 2) Find the time $t=\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$. 3) Range $=u\cos\theta\times t$.
cards.hint: Start with the initial velocity components.

cards.front: What is the formula for the maximum height of a projectile launched from level ground, and what do the symbols mean?
cards.back: $h=\frac{(u\sin\theta)^2}{2g}$, where $u\sin\theta$ is the initial vertical velocity in $\text{m\,s}^{-1}$, $g=9.81\,\text{m\,s}^{-2}$ and $h$ is in $\text{m}$.
cards.hint: What is the vertical velocity at the highest point?

cards.front: Which equation gives the time to fall for a ball launched horizontally from a height, and what does each symbol mean?
cards.back: $s_y=\frac{1}{2}gt^2$, so $t=\sqrt{\frac{2s_y}{g}}$. $s_y$ is the height in $\text{m}$, $g=9.81\,\text{m\,s}^{-2}$ and $t$ is in $\text{s}$.
cards.hint: What is the starting vertical velocity in this case?

cards.front: A ball is thrown horizontally at $15\,\text{m\,s}^{-1}$ from a cliff 19.6 m high. What is its time of flight?
cards.back: $2.0\,\text{s}$, from $t=\sqrt{\frac{2\times19.6}{9.81}}$. The horizontal speed does not affect this time.

cards.front: A ball is launched from level ground at $20\,\text{m\,s}^{-1}$ and $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. What is its range?
cards.back: About $35\,\text{m}$. The horizontal component is $17.3\,\text{m\,s}^{-1}$ and the time of flight is $2.04\,\text{s}$, so $17.3\times2.04\approx35\,\text{m}$.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to think a projectile needs a forward force to keep moving sideways?
cards.back: With no horizontal force acting, the **horizontal velocity** stays constant. A projectile keeps moving sideways without any forward force.
cards.hint: What happens to horizontal velocity when no horizontal force acts?

cards.front: Why is the speed of a projectile least at its highest point, ignoring air resistance?
cards.back: At the top the velocity is purely horizontal, with no vertical component, so the speed is only the horizontal part, which is the smallest value.
cards.hint: Consider the vertical velocity at the top.

cards.front: Which launch angle gives the longest range from level ground at a fixed speed?
cards.back: $45^{\circ}$ gives the longest range. The horizontal and vertical components are balanced at this angle.
cards.hint: Think about how the two components trade off against each other.

cards.front: How do ranges compare for launches at $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ with the same speed?
cards.back: They are **equal**. Launch angles that add up to $90^{\circ}$ give the same range at the same speed.
cards.hint: Compare the two sets of components.

cards.front: Why does air resistance reduce the range of a real projectile?
cards.back: It acts against the velocity, reducing horizontal velocity and maximum height. The projectile covers less horizontal distance before it lands.
cards.hint: Which direction does air resistance act compared with the motion?

cards.front: What is the range of a projectile?
cards.back: The **range** is the horizontal distance from the launch point to the point where the projectile lands at the same height.
**Air resistance** is the force exerted by the air on a moving object, acting in the direction opposite to its velocity.
